candidates.label: Samothrace (island)
candidates.support: An island in the north Aegean Sea, south of Thrace, with a town at its northern end where ships could anchor for the night. Pleiades, OpenBible.info and Wikidata agree on the island, known today as Samothraki.

summary.text: Samothrace is a mountainous island in the northern Aegean Sea, south of Thrace, long known for its sanctuary of the Cabeiri, gods whose mystery cult rivaled the famous mysteries of Eleusis; King Philip of Macedon and his wife Olympias were said to have been initiated there. Acts records that on the voyage from Troas to Philippi, Paul and his companions made a straight course to Samothrace and continued the next day to Neapolis; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that at the island's northern end was a town where the ship could anchor for the night.

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports that the island's name reflects its height, towering over the neighboring island of Imbros, and that it is mentioned in Homer's Iliad as the seat of the god Poseidon. The sculpture known as the Winged Victory of Samothrace, discovered at the island's Cabirion sanctuary in 1863 and today in the Louvre museum, is dated by the Louvre to the early second century BC, possibly created at Rhodes; the encyclopedia, reflecting an older, since-revised view, instead dated the statue's erection to around 300 BC, crediting it to the Macedonian ruler Demetrius Poliorcetes.

The encyclopedia notes that the Roman writer Pliny described the island as a difficult place to anchor, though ancient sailors preferred to find anchorage somewhere for the night rather than risk sailing in the dark; it also observes that on Paul's return journey a landing on Samothrace may have been made, though Acts gives no details of that leg of the voyage.

scripture.textWEB: Setting sail therefore from Troas, we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the day following to Neapolis;

politicalHistory.note: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography records that "in Pliny's time Samothrace was a free state," referring to the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, who wrote in the mid-to-late first century AD; no cited source dates when this status began or whether it changed across the span this map covers.
